1:
Keil sets the chapter in place: what begins here is the conclusion of the covenant in Moab, the renewal of what was concluded at Horeb — first instructions to set up the law solemnly in Canaan after crossing Jordan, then an exposition of blessing and curse as they would fall according to the people's attitude to it, and last a solemn address setting the choice of blessing and life before the nation. The opening command to keep the whole law uses the infinitive absolute for the imperative, and standing at the head it governs what follows. Henry fastens on who gives the charge. It is pressed with all authority, by Moses with the elders, the rulers of each tribe, and again by Moses and the priests, so it comes from the man who was king in Jeshurun and from their lords both spiritual and temporal. Lest the people think it was only Moses, an old and dying man, who made such ado about religion, or only priests whose trade it was and whose maintenance came out of it, the elders are joined in — men of business, likely to remain so long after Moses was gone. Moses, having put some of his honour on them, joins them in commission with himself, as Paul sometimes joins Silvanus and Timothy in his letters. All who have power over others should use it for the support of religion; for though the supreme power provide the best of laws, if magistrates, ministers and masters of families do not execute their offices, it will come to little.

The second direction is to register the words of the law on entering the land, once only, in token of taking possession under its conditions — a solemnity Henry compares with the ratification at Sinai. Two things strike him. The monument was to be very mean — rough unhewn stone plastered over, not polished marble, nor tables of brass, but common plaster upon stone; and the writing not fine, to be admired by the curious, but plain, so that he who runs may read. The word of God needs not be set off by the art of man, nor embellished with the enticing words of man's wisdom. Yet the inscription was to be great, being all the words of this law, and what that covered is disputed. Some understand only the covenant lately made; some the curses of this chapter, the rather because the stones stood on Ebal; some the whole book. Henry thinks the heap might be large enough to carry so copious an inscription — unless only the ten commandments were written there, as a copy of the rolls laid up in the ark. Clarke's summary runs to the same order: the law written on stones at the entry, an altar of unhewn stones with burnt and peace offerings, six tribes for blessing on Gerizim and six for cursing on Ebal.

Calvin puts the command in a class with those he has treated before. God would have his precepts written on the door-posts and the borders of their garments, so they might constantly meet the eye; here a monument at the very entrance of the land, from which the people might learn on what terms they dwelt in it. The purpose is that knowledge of the law should not be obscured or obliterated by carelessness, and so its sum is inscribed in a conspicuous place. From this he draws the likeness he has already noted between private houses and the whole country: as the precepts on doors admonished each man that his house was sacred to God, so the writing at the border told whoever entered that the land itself was the sanctuary of heavenly doctrine, and might stir their zeal for pure worship. The direction that the writing be plain he takes to have one object — to take away the excuse of ignorance.
2:
Keil takes the day named as a term of latitude, meaning the time when Israel had entered and taken possession; Gill agrees the order was not executed until after Ai was destroyed. On the stones Clarke observes that no number is given — possibly twelve, possibly only enough for the writing — and suggests that plaster them with plaster might as well be cement them with cement, this being a durable monument; the usual practice of a rude heap without mortar made particular directions necessary where that method was not followed. He reports too the suggestion that the letters stood in relief with the cement filling the spaces, eastern inscriptions being often cut so. Keil takes the plainer view: the writing was not cut into the stone and afterwards covered, but painted on the coat of lime, as in Egypt, where walls and monuments were coated before the figures were laid on.

Where the stones stood is contested. Clarke notes that the Samaritan reads Gerizim where the Hebrew reads Ebal, Kennicott defending the Samaritan and Parry and Verschuir the Hebrew, many thinking Kennicott unanswerable and suspecting a corruption made out of enmity to the Samaritans. What all sides allow is the character of the hills: Gerizim abounds with springs, gardens and orchards and is covered with verdure, while Ebal is as naked and barren as a rock, which made the one fit for blessing and the other for cursing. Keil will have none of the Samaritan reading, calling it an arbitrary alteration. Wesley presses the theology of the site: the law was written on the mount of cursing to signify that a curse is due to its violators, and that none can expect justification from a law by whose sentence all are accused; the sacrifices show there is no deliverance from it but by the blood of Christ, who was made a curse for us. What was written is disputed likewise. Gill denies it was the whole book and suspects a summary, perhaps the ten commandments, noting that Josephus thought the blessings and curses were meant; Clarke, after all the ingenuity spent on it, holds the word means the blessings and curses of this chapter and the next, themselves a good epitome of the whole law. Ellicott says flatly the ten commandments, all else being the application of the Decalogue to a particular people; and on the direction to write very plainly he passes on the rabbinic gloss, in seventy languages, with the notion that at Sinai the law was heard in all tongues at once — a strange refraction of Pentecost, the founding of Jerusalem having effects exactly opposite to the founding of Babel.

The altar comes next, and Calvin reads it as thanksgiving required at their first entrance; Joshua built one of whole stones over which no iron was lifted. The prohibition of tooled work he explains by its danger: a permanent altar would have occasioned superstition, and the exception come to be more regarded than the perpetual law. That is why the nine tribes and a half were so wroth over the altar built by Jordan that they were ready to destroy their brethren, until the builders pleaded it a memorial and not for sacrifice — good expounders of the law, Calvin says, who counted it inexpiable to leave an altar that might withdraw posterity from the one sanctuary. Ellicott dismisses the theory that the stones came from Jordan, and defines the offerings: the burnt offering is the dedication of a man's life to God, the peace offering for deliverance already granted, and being the only kind the worshipper and his family might eat, it naturally accompanied rejoicing. Wesley draws the halves together: by the law on the stones God spoke to them, and by the altar they spoke to God, so communion was kept up. Gill notes that some made the altar itself the inscribed stone.
9:
The charge is renewed, and Ellicott notes that where the opening verse had Moses with the elders, this has him with the priests. The word rendered take heed occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament, and the declaration that this day thou art become the people of the Lord he glosses from the maxim that God's commandments should be before a man's eyes daily, as though he had that day entered into covenant. What is chiefly in view is the passage of Jordan, which he thinks pledged Israel to the law more completely than Sinai itself had, God having gone further with them and given them a more distinct position, so they needed more than ever to remember whose they were. Calvin grounds the exhortation on that same favour of adoption: nothing should have stirred them to obedience more than a love more than paternal; hence the inference that being received as God's own they were bound to keep his statutes — as Paul teaches that we are redeemed from all iniquity, that Christ might purify to himself a peculiar people zealous of good works. Since the priests were now appointed, from whose lips the doctrine of the law was to be sought, they come forward in God's name, engaging Israel not only to answer his calls but to obey his ministers. Gill notes that these were the lawful priests, whose business was to teach the statutes and see them kept; Wesley, that they became the Lord's people by this solemn renewing of the covenant.

Henry sets the scene. In the part of Canaan that afterwards fell to Ephraim two mountains lay near together with a valley between, and on the facing slopes the tribes drew up, six on each, near enough at the foot that the priests standing between could be heard. When silence was proclaimed, one of them pronounced a malediction aloud, and all on the Ebal side said Amen, those further off taking the signal from those within hearing; then the contrary sentence came, and Gerizim answered it. Keil describes the act as a transfer to the land itself of the sanctions of the law, the favourable side falling to the tribes sprung from Jacob's two wives and the other to Reuben with Zilpah's sons, and Zebulun with Dan and Naphtali. Ellicott adds from the Jewish account that priests, Levites and ark stayed below between the hills.

What the division meant is disputed. Ellicott holds the usual phrasing misleading, since it was not that six tribes blessed and six cursed their brethren: the rule is explicit that all the people say Amen, so the sense must be that these stood on Gerizim to receive the benediction for the whole and these on Ebal the doom, the twelve divided equally because all lay equally open to either. He observes that strictly seven stood on Gerizim, Joseph including Ephraim and Manasseh, and that the arrangement was an amphitheatre, the speakers in the centre below. He notes too that Ebal carried both the law which inflicts the sentence and the altar representing him who bore it, so those receiving the doom stand on the same slope as the Redeemer. Calvin confesses he does not know why those six were chosen, and finds no force in the opinion that descent from free mothers gave the higher place, since Reuben the firstborn was ranked with the handmaids' sons — unless so degraded for ignominy. He is not curious about it, since both were offered in the nation's name, witnessing their common consent. Henry, who does take the free-women reading, notes that Levi stands among them to teach ministers to apply to themselves what they preach to others, and that the Levites utter the maledictions too, since they must separate the precious from the vile: a minister must press the terrors of the law as well as the comforts of the gospel.
12:
Clarke queries the preposition. The particle rendered upon is sometimes translated by or beside, and he thinks it must be so here, since when the direction was executed the people stood not on the mountains but over against them on the plain; Wesley renders it the same way, and notes that Joseph stands here for both Manasseh and Ephraim, reckoned as one because Levi is numbered, whereas where the land is divided and Levi omitted they count as two. Who spoke has an agreed answer. Gill and Wesley point out that the whole tribe of Levi stood on Gerizim, so those who pronounced the words must be its priests, stationed in the valley and turning toward one hill or the other as they spoke. Keil defines the term likewise: the Levites here are not all the tribe but those in whom the character of Levi was most manifest, the levitical priests; and the people's Amen takes the sentence on themselves, as in every oath.

The unrecorded blessings trouble three. Gill takes the silence for design: they were not to be had from the law, and it is meant to put men on seeking them elsewhere, in Christ, though he supposes they were spoken in the same form as the curses and simply reversed. Calvin thinks the Spirit may be indirectly rebuking the people, since when they ought to have embraced the promised reward their ungodliness deprived them of that honour; yet the forms of cursing teach what course was to be observed in blessing, for when God condemns transgressors we may infer that blessedness is laid up for his true servants. Wesley puts it evangelically: as many as were under the law were under the curse, and it was an honour reserved for Christ to bless us and do what the law could not, so that in his sermon on the mount, the true Gerizim, there are blessings only. He asks how the people could say Amen to a curse, and answers that it was a profession of faith in its truth and an acknowledgment of its equity — not that it shall be so only, but that it is just.

The list is selective, and Calvin and Ellicott both say so. Ellicott finds the first curse pointing to the opening commandments of the first table and the second to the first of the second, then arranges the rest: duty to parents, the rights of neighbours, of the blind and of the unprotected; four precepts on purity; two at the end on slander and treachery. The offences are examples of whole classes, and the twelve may answer to the number of the tribes, as Keil also counts them. Calvin presses harder by noting who is missing: no separate curse falls on blasphemers, perjurers, Sabbath-breakers or adulterers, so certain crimes were selected to teach that no transgression would go unpunished; by naming the graven image God defends his worship from every pollution, and the curse reaches every breach of the first table. What holds it together, Calvin thinks, is secrecy. The image is put in a hidden place, the theft escapes men's knowledge, the acts of uncleanness are concealed the more for their filthiness, and the murderer cursed is the one who sheds innocent blood for hire, a compact not easily brought to light. No concealment will profit, since shame will be discovered at his tribunal; the people are summoned there to be held to duty not by fear of penalty only but for conscience' sake — which shows he delivered no merely political law, but one requiring sincerity of heart. Gill and Ellicott read the cases alike, the landmark shifted backward to steal ground, the blind man taken as any who is in the dark and deceived. Clarke adds that these things were forbidden already, with penalties understood, but here God declares more openly that the breaker is cursed.
19:
Gill runs through the closing offences with one thread in view: these incestuous and brutal couplings may be supposed done in secret, and he who smites his neighbour privately kills without the murder being known, though God's curse overtakes him at last. He notes an alternative reading, taken by some of smiting with the tongue, secret backbiting and slander — the Targum has it of the third tongue — and Ellicott passes on the same gloss. Wesley keeps the plain sense of killing but widens it: it includes murder under colour of law, of all affronts to God the greatest, so cursed is he who any way helps to condemn an innocent person. On the last particular curse Gill reports a like division: some understand a hired assassin, some a judge bribed to condemn the innocent, another a false witness who swears away a man's life for reward.

The closing curse turns on a word absent from the printed text. Clarke observes that the term rendered all is missing from the common Hebrew, but stands in the Samaritan, in six manuscripts collated by Kennicott and De Rossi, in the Chaldee paraphrase, in the Greek, and in Paul's quotation; and he passes on Jerome's charge that the Jews suppressed it lest it appear they were bound to fulfil every precept. He also reproduces Kennicott's table setting the twelve curses against the ten commandments, the graven image answering to the first four and so on to the summary curse and the tenth — adding his own verdict, that many will think the arrangement fanciful. On the standing of the tribes Clarke adds a remark. Blessing was the more honourable office and fell to the children of the two wives, cursing to the handmaids' sons; and since six were needed on each side, two of the honourable had to join the four. Zebulun was chosen as Leah's youngest, and Reuben because, though the eldest, he had forfeited the birthright — so that his posterity stood degraded, and were obliged to pronounce the very curse that fell upon their father's own sin.

The last sentence gathers up the rest, and three read it as the law's verdict on all men. Calvin observes that although God had threatened secret sins designedly, so men should not fear human judgments only, the conclusion extends the same sentence to iniquities of every kind, declaring that whoever does not perform what the law requires is accursed. From this Paul rightly infers that as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse; for let the most perfect man come forward, and however diligently he has striven he will have offended somewhere — and whoever keeps the whole law yet offends in one point is guilty of all. Paul does not quote the words exactly, but the sense is the same, since all are condemned who have not fulfilled what the law contains; and to this the Israelites were commanded to assent, acknowledging themselves lost. So too, he adds, we must be struck with the same despair, that embracing the grace of Christ we may be delivered, since he was made accursed for us. Wesley says the same in a sentence: to this we must all say Amen, owning ourselves under the curse, and that we must have perished had Christ not been made a curse for us. Ellicott quotes the comment that here the whole law is summed up and taken on them with a curse and an oath, and draws the same conclusion: the blessing of Gerizim cannot be had except through him who bore the curse of Ebal. He adds a point of grammar worth having: in all these sentences the verb is wanting, so cursed is he would be the more correct English — they are not imprecations so much as declarations of fact. Gill adds that the obedience required is perfect.
